---
title: "Background: the hold test as a linear program"
subtitle: "The same support question posed as linear programs that work unchanged in 2D and 3D, with a witness, a certificate, a margin and force limits."
lightbox: true
---

**What this explains.** [Deciding support exactly](bg-exact-hold-test.qmd)
answers "can these contacts hold the box?" by enumeration, which only works
in the plane. This page poses the same question as **linear programs (LPs)**.
The LPs don't care whether wrenches have 3 components (planar) or 6
(spatial). The 3D version therefore only adds a builder for its generators,
and the LPs and the solver stay the same. The LPs also do two things the
enumeration cannot: they handle **limits on the manipulator's force** and
**margins against a set of disturbances**. Read the exact-test page first;
this one reuses its notation and its running example (a square box on the
floor, μ = 0.2, forces in mg, moments in mg·ℓ). Every number here comes from
`scripts/bg_hold_lp.py`, which solves the LPs with HiGHS (dual simplex,
float64).

## 1. One backbone, two dimensions

The LPs take four pieces of data:

| Data | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $W \in \R^{d\times k}$ | generators: one column per friction-cone edge at each support point, as a wrench |
| $\text{need} \in \R^d$ | the wrench the contacts must supply (minus gravity, minus any known external wrench) |
| $B\,\lambda \le f_{\max}$ (optional) | force limits, one row per limited contact |
| $u_1, \dots, u_J$ (optional) | disturbance directions for the margin |

The unknowns are the edge weights $\lambda \in \R^k$, $\lambda \ge 0$. Only the
builder of $W$ and need knows the dimension:

| | Planar (now) | Spatial (3D, later) |
|---|---|---|
| Wrench, $d$ | $(f_x, f_z, \tau_y/\ell)$, $d = 3$ | $(f, \tau/\ell)$, $d = 6$ |
| Friction cone at a point | exactly 2 edges, $n \pm \mu t$ | circular cone; inner pyramid with $m$ edges $n + \mu(\cos\theta_j t_1 + \sin\theta_j t_2)$ |
| Support points of a contact | the 2 endpoints of the contact segment | the vertices of the contact polygon |
| Each edge's normal component | 1 (so a contact's normal force is the sum of its weights) | 1 (same) |
| LPs, solver, checks | shared | shared |

The pyramid's edges lie *on* the circular cone, so the pyramid sits inside
it. A box the pyramid holds is really held. The approximation can only
reject, never accept wrongly, and 8 edges keep at least
$\cos(\pi/8) = 92\%$ of the friction in every direction. The reduction to a
polygon's vertices is the same linearity argument as for a segment's
endpoints: a force's moment is linear in its point of application.

## 2. LP-1: feasibility, with a witness and a certificate

The direct LP, "find $\lambda \ge 0$ with $W\lambda = \text{need}$", has no
solution exactly when the answer is no. A solver then reports "infeasible",
and some solvers report nothing more. The fix is to make the LP always
solvable by adding slack $s^\pm \ge 0$ that pays for any mismatch:
$$
\text{LP-1:}\qquad \delta \;=\; \min_{\lambda,\, s^+,\, s^- \,\ge\, 0}\; \mathbf 1^\top s^+ + \mathbf 1^\top s^-
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad W\lambda + s^+ - s^- = \text{need}.
$$

- **It always has a solution:** $\lambda = 0$, $s^+ = \max(\text{need}, 0)$, $s^- = \max(-\text{need}, 0)$ satisfies it, and $\delta \ge 0$.
- **Its optimum is a distance:** $\delta = \min_{\lambda \ge 0}\|W\lambda - \text{need}\|_1$, the ℓ₁ distance from need to the cone $C$. So $\delta = 0$ means supported.
- **Yes comes with a witness.** The simplex method returns a *basic*
  optimal solution, with at most $d$ nonzero variables. When $\delta = 0$,
  those are at most $d$ generators that hold the box. This is
  Carathéodory's theorem again, now produced by the solver.

**No comes with a certificate.** The LP dual is

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Dual of LP-1.** $\displaystyle \delta = \max_{y}\ \text{need}^\top y \quad\text{s.t.}\quad W^\top y \le 0,\ \ -\mathbf 1 \le y \le \mathbf 1.$
:::

If $\delta > 0$, the optimal $y$ has $W^\top y \le 0$ and
$\text{need}^\top y = \delta > 0$. So $z = -y$ has $z\cdot w_i \ge 0$ for every
generator and $z\cdot\text{need} < 0$: the Farkas certificate of the exact-test
page. A simplex solver has $y$ in hand at the end, at no extra cost.

*Example.* Flat box on both corners: $\delta = 0$, and the witness is
$\lambda_{A_+} = \lambda_{B_-} = \tfrac12$, the same as the exact test's.
Corner A alone: $\delta = 1.0$, with dual $y = (-1, 1, -1)$. Then
$z = (1, -1, 1)$ gives $z\cdot w_{A_\pm} = 0$ and $z\cdot\text{need} = -1 < 0$.
That is the exact test's certificate $(1,-1,1)/\sqrt3$, unscaled. A grid
search over $\lambda$ confirms the ℓ₁ distance 1.0.

## 3. LP-2: the margin, as exit distances

The exact test's margin is a Euclidean distance, and a Euclidean ball is
not a polytope, so it needs a second-order cone program, not an LP. A
polytope of disturbances is an LP. The natural one is the ℓ₁ ball, whose
$2d$ corners are the pure disturbances $\pm e_i$: a pure sideways push, a
pure lift, a pure twist.

For a direction $u$, the **exit distance** is how far need can move along
$u$ before leaving the cone:
$$
\text{LP-2:}\qquad t(u) \;=\; \max_{\lambda \ge 0,\ 0 \le t \le T}\; t
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad W\lambda = \text{need} + t\,u .
$$
The cap $T$ keeps the LP bounded when the cone never ends in that direction
(the code uses $T = 10$; §6 says why).
Here $u$ is the extra wrench the contacts must supply; a disturbance of
$-t\,u$ acts on the box.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Claim.** If need $\in C$, the largest ℓ₁ ball around need that fits in $C$ has radius $\min_i\, t(\pm e_i)$.
:::

*Why.* The ℓ₁ ball of radius $r$ is the convex hull of its $2d$ corners
$\text{need} \pm r\,e_i$. A convex set contains it exactly when it contains
the corners. Along each direction, the points of $C$ form an interval
$[0, t(u)]$, because $C$ is convex and contains need. So the corners fit iff
$r \le t(\pm e_i)$ for every $i$. Any polytope $D$ of disturbances works the
same way, with one LP per corner of $D$.

Together with LP-1, this gives a **signed ℓ₁ margin**: $\min_i t(\pm e_i)$
inside the cone and $-\delta$ outside. It is the same construction as the
exact test's signed Euclidean distance, with a different norm.

![Exit distances of the flat box along the six pure directions, from LP-2. (a) On two corners: the margin is the sideways push, 0.2·mg = μ·mg. Pushing down (+f<sub>z</sub>) never breaks support; lifting by the full weight (−f<sub>z</sub>) and twisting by mg·ℓ (±τ, the box tips) do. (b) With the disk pushing on the left face at the height of the center of mass, and its normal force limited to 0.5·mg. The disk raises the +f<sub>x</sub> exit to 0.72, but the margin stays 0.2: the disk pushes only one way, so the −f<sub>x</sub> exit is still set by floor friction alone.](media/bg_lp_exits.svg){.lightbox}

**Reading the flat box.** The ℓ₁ margin is 0.2, exactly μ: the smallest
pure push that breaks support. The Euclidean margin was 0.196, because the
worst Euclidean direction mixes a push with a slight lift. The ℓ₁ number is
easier to state, and its directions are the ones an engineer would test.
Both depend on $\ell$, since it sets how a moment trades against a force.

## 4. LP-3: force limits

The disk's force is unbounded in the cone model, so with the disk in the
formation the cone can fill all of $\R^3$ and the margin becomes infinite
(the exact test reports a cap). Every edge has unit normal component, so a
contact's normal force is the sum of its edge weights. A limit is one more
row:
$$
\sum_{j \in \text{edges of contact } c} \lambda_j \;\le\; f_{\max,c}.
$$
Add it to LP-1 and LP-2. The feasible wrenches then form a cone (the
environment's contacts) plus a polytope (the manipulator's). Directions the
disk helps now have finite exits: in panel (b), $t(+f_x) = 0.72$. That is
0.5 from the disk plus 0.22 of floor friction, because the disk's friction
also presses the box onto the floor ($0.2 \times 1.1$). The dual gains one
multiplier per limit, and the certificate becomes $(z, v)$ with $v \ge 0$:
still a few inequalities anyone can check.

This settles the open item "finite margins with the disk" (Decision 6).
Since Nov 7 the gate uses the simulator's actuator limits: the disk's two
motors (±1 N each) must supply its force on the box plus its own weight,
which gives two rows per motor ([step 2](02-hold-gate.qmd#gate)). OpenArm's
limits replace them when it arrives.

## 5. Robustness, again for free

The robust versions are the same as on the exact-test page, now as more
LPs of the same shape:

- **Friction:** use the lower end of the friction interval.
- **Mass and center of mass:** one need per corner of the uncertainty box.
  The verdict and margin are the worst over those needs.

The LPs all have the same size, so they batch with `vmap`: over poses, over
needs and over directions.

## 6. Solving it

The LPs are tiny and dense: $d = 3$ or $6$ rows, tens to a hundred-odd
columns. Many of them are solved at once, and the interesting ones sit on
the support boundary, where they are degenerate. That rules some methods in
and some out:

| Method | Returns | Fit |
|---|---|---|
| **Simplex** | a vertex (witness with ≤ d generators) and the dual (certificate) | Best fit: a handful of pivots; exact up to rounding; Bland's rule avoids cycling at degenerate points |
| Interior point | an interior point; duals | Workable: always converges in a few dozen iterations; the witness is dense, and the certificate needs care near the boundary |
| First-order (PDHG, e.g. MPAX) | an approximate point | Poor fit: built for huge sparse LPs. On ours it converges slowly near the boundary and cannot certify "no" when it stops early. In step 2, MPAX falsely rejected about 193 of 416 supported cases near the boundary |

**Solvers that run inside JAX** (so the test can be jitted and vmapped with
the rest of the planner): **linrax** (Georgia Tech, ACC 2026), a two-phase
tableau simplex method with Bland's rule, is the only one we found.
Patrick Kidger's Lineax and Optimistix do linear solves and nonlinear
optimisation, not LPs. JAXopt is no longer maintained. qpax, an interior
point method, was surveyed but not needed. **HiGHS** (via SciPy) stays
outside JAX as the float64 reference that checks every answer in the tests.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Decision (Nov 6, 2026).** The backbone is adopted and solved by linrax
(`cmg/src/cmg/physics/hold_lp.py`, `PlanarHold(method="lp")`, commit
`e29d96f`). Two caveats and one option are on record:

- **linrax has no license file** (neither its repository nor its PyPI
  package). cmg depends on it as published, pinned to 0.3.0, without copying
  its code. This is accepted; linrax stays.
- **linrax returns no dual.** The dual is recovered at the end from its final
  basis $B$, by solving $B^\top y = c_B$; LP-1's certificate is then $-y$.
- **Set inclusion stays an option** for the margin, beside the ℓ₁ margin and
  the exact test's Euclidean one: the corners of a disturbance polytope $D$
  as LP-2 directions (§3). *Chosen Nov 7:* set inclusion, with $D$ the ℓ₁
  unit ball by default ([step 2](02-hold-gate.qmd#gate)).
:::

**linrax's pivot loop, replaced.** linrax takes no iteration cap. Its
whole pivot loop, though, is one small function that `linprog` looks up when
it is traced, so `hold_lp` swaps in its own version at import (checked
against the pinned 0.3.0). The tableau and the entering rule stay the same,
with three changes:

- **An iteration cap**, 300 pivots per phase. Under `vmap` the loop runs
  until the slowest LP of the batch finishes, so a single LP that never
  finishes hangs them all. That happened on 3D cones (below).
- **Bland's leaving rule.** Ties in the ratio test go to the basic variable
  with the lowest index. linrax took the lowest row instead, which does
  not rule out cycling, and one 3D LP cycled.
- **Artificial rows marked with ≥.** After phase 1 the artificial columns
  are deleted, and the first artificial index equals the index of the
  right-hand-side column. linrax's test used >, so it missed that row, and
  on the flat box it returned a slack of −1 and called it optimal.

**Making it work in float32.** All computations stay in float32. Each of
these measures fixed, or measurably helped with, a failure the tests found:

1. **Spread the right-hand side.** A planar need from gravity alone is
   $(0, 1, 0)$, with two zero rows. The equality rows are rotated by the
   Householder reflection $H$ that maps need to
   $\lvert\text{need}\rvert(1,\dots,1)/\sqrt{d}$. $H$ is orthogonal, so
   the LP is the same ($Ax = b \iff HAx = Hb$), perfectly conditioned, and
   every right-hand side is positive. The dual maps back by $y = Hy'$. It
   first worked around the artificial-row bug above. It stays because it
   still tests slightly better: 5 uncertain answers in 768 3D cases against
   10 without it.
2. **Recompute the primal from the final basis**, by one solve with $B$,
   rather than reading it off the tableau, which carries the rounding of
   every pivot.
3. **Pivot tolerance $10^{-4}$.** linrax's default, $10^{-6}$, is both its
   smallest allowed pivot and its optimality tolerance. In float32 it pivots
   on noise: on 600 random LPs it gave 19 wrong answers, and none at
   $10^{-4}$.
4. **Cap exits at 10** ($mg$, $mg\ell$), not $10^3$. The cap row reads
   $t/T \le 1$. With $T = 10^3$ its coefficient fell to the pivot threshold
   during pivoting, the ratio test skipped the row, and linrax returned
   negative weights. Ten times the weight in a pure direction counts as
   unlimited for margins of order μ.

Every answer is then checked independently of the solver, with elementwise
products (no reduced-precision TF32 on GPUs). A witness is checked by its
residual, a certificate by its signs, and an exit by its weights. A failed
exit check sets that exit to 0, so a solver error can shrink the margin but
not enlarge it.

**Benchmark** (step 2: 1,000 random cases and 416 within 2 mm of disk
height of the support boundary; reference HiGHS in float64; all float32):

| Device | Exact test, near boundary | LP, near boundary | ms per 256: exact / LP-1 / LP with margins |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU | 390 of 416 | 386 of 416 | 4.1 / 2.7 / 6.3 |
| GPU | 389 of 416 | 383 of 416 | 1.5 / 2.0 / 2.5 |

Both get all 1,000 random cases right. Near the boundary the two make the
same 12 confident mistakes. These are poses where both certify "not
supported" with margins of −0.7 to −1 while HiGHS says supported, so the
inputs differ upstream of the test, not in the solvers. Every other
disagreement is a pose reported as uncertain and rejected, the safe
direction. These poses sit where the cone is nearly flat and a witness
needs weights of 60–190 times the weight, beyond what float32 can check to
$10^{-5}$. An earlier run that trusted linrax's own feasibility flag scored
404, but nothing checked that flag, and it accepted a pose that HiGHS
rejects.

**In 3D.** The same code was run on a cube touched by up to four contacts
(face patches, edges and points; 8-edge pyramids; $d = 6$, up to 128
generators; 1,024 cases batched with `vmap`; float32 on CPU). The results:

- Nothing hangs. linrax's own loop had cycled and stalled the whole batch.
- Nothing is certified wrongly.
- 763 of 768 random cases and 255 of 256 near-boundary cases come out right.
- The other 5 random cases are supported but end "uncertain", which is
  safe.
- The one near-boundary miss is a false acceptance 0.1% outside the
  boundary.
- LP-1 takes 40 ms per 256 cases, and the full test with 12 exits about
  300 ms.

The uncertain cases come from float32 rounding that builds up in linrax's
dense tableau over the longer pivot sequences of 3D cones. They are not
caused by the cap: the same cases stay uncertain at 5,000 pivots. The
standard cure is *reinversion*: rebuild the tableau from the final basis
($B^{-1}A$ and $B^{-1}b$, computed fresh) and continue. It is planned for
when the 3D build arrives.

Since Nov 7 the LPs are the default gate, with the simulator's actuator
limits and the ℓ₁ margin ([step 2](02-hold-gate.qmd#gate)). The
planar and spatial builders never see the solver: it sits behind
`solve(c, A_eq, b_eq, A_ub, b_ub)`, which returns the primal, the dual and
the status.

## 7. The exact test and the LPs, side by side

| | Exact test (plane only) | LPs (any dimension) |
|---|---|---|
| Yes | witness, ≤ 3 generators | witness, ≤ d generators (basic solution) |
| No | Farkas plane from a candidate list | Farkas plane from the dual |
| Margin | signed Euclidean distance | signed ℓ₁ distance, or any polytope of disturbances |
| Force limits | no | yes (one row each) |
| 3D | no (about 5×10⁹ subsets) | yes (6 rows) |
| Cost per 256 cases, float32 (CPU / GPU) | 4.8 / 1.6 ms | 2.4 / 1.8 ms (linrax, feasibility only) |

In the plane, the two agree on yes and no wherever floating point allows,
and the exact test remains a cross-check.

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 1. Why can LP-1 never report "infeasible"?
$\lambda = 0$ with $s^\pm$ equal to the positive and negative parts of need
satisfies every constraint, and the objective is at least 0. So the LP is
feasible and bounded, and the solver always ends with an optimal basis and
its dual.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 2. In 3D with an 8-edge pyramid, can the test accept a pose that real friction cannot hold?
No. The pyramid lies inside the true friction cone, so every force it allows
is a real force. The error is one-sided: it may reject a pose that needs
more than 92% of the available friction in an unlucky direction.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 3. In panel (b), why does adding the disk not raise the margin?
The margin is the smallest exit. The disk can only push in +x, so it cannot
help resist a disturbance that needs −x force from the contacts; floor
friction alone sets $t(-f_x) = 0.2$. A second disk on the other face, or
a gripper, would.
:::
